nameStory: The Dark Shadow Lichen gets its name from the distinctive black, granular bumps called isidia that dot its surface like stubble on a face. It's also sometimes called the "five o'clock shadow" lichen because these dark specks give it the same dusky appearance as facial hair emerging through skin.
description: Dark Shadow Lichen is a crusty, flat organism that's actually two life forms living together - a fungus and an algae in partnership. It forms neat, circular rosettes up to 2 inches across on sun-baked rocks, made up of tiny flat lobes that hug tightly to the stone surface. Each lobe is only about half a millimeter wide, creating an intricate pattern that looks almost like a miniature succulent plant pressed flat against the rock.

idTips.label: Black granular bumps
idTips.description: Look for distinctive black, sand-like granules scattered across the surface and edges - these isidia feel slightly rough to the touch and are the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Rosette growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms neat, circular patterns up to 2 inches across that radiate outward from the center like flower petals

idTips.label: Tiny flat lobes
idTips.description: Individual lobes are extremely narrow (about 0.5mm) and feel smooth except for the granular isidia, lying completely flat against the rock

idTips.label: Rock-hugging habit
idTips.description: Adheres so tightly to rock surfaces that it's nearly impossible to peel off without damaging - feels like it's painted on

idTips.label: Sun-exposed location
idTips.description: Almost always found on rocks that get direct sunlight for much of the day, especially on vertical or slanted surfaces

habitat: Look for Dark Shadow Lichen on sun-exposed rocky outcrops, stone walls, and boulders throughout New England, with a particular fondness for sandstone surfaces. It thrives on vertical rock faces and slanted surfaces that catch plenty of direct sunlight. You'll often find it sharing space with other rock-dwelling lichens on everything from roadside stone walls to natural cliff faces.

seasonality.spring: The black isidia become more prominent as the lichen begins its growing season, making identification easier on warming rocks.
seasonality.summer: Most active growth period when the rosette patterns are most clearly defined and the contrast between the lichen body and black granules is strongest.
seasonality.fall: Still easily identifiable as the lichen remains active in cool weather, with isidia clearly visible against the changing light.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round on snow-free rock faces, though may appear slightly duller; the distinctive black granules still provide reliable identification.

funFact: This tiny lichen is one of the most well-traveled organisms on Earth, naturally occurring on every continent except Antarctica and thriving in environments from African deserts to Arctic tundra - all while never moving from its chosen rock!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other shadow lichens in the same genus, but the abundant black isidia scattered across both the center and edges of the lobes are distinctive. Memory trick: if it looks like it needs a shave with all those black stubble-like bumps, it's the Dark Shadow Lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "lichen," this organism is actually a successful partnership between a fungus and an algae that has been so evolutionarily successful it's found on six continents. The name "shadow" doesn't refer to shade-loving habits - quite the opposite, as these lichens prefer sunny exposures.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Dark Shadow Lichen is easily recognized by its abundant black isidia that cover both the center and edges of the lobes. The Orange-cored and Red-cored Shadow Lichens show colorful centers when broken, while others like the Hairy Shadow Lichen have hair-like projections instead of granular bumps. The black isidia make Dark Shadow Lichen the "stubbly" member of the shadow lichen family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its bright orange pycnidial contents - most other wreath lichens in this genus have white, yellow, or red cores instead.
Among the shadow lichens in its genus, Pom-pom Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its small size and abundant powdery soredia clusters.
Among its wreath lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen is distinguished by having the white soredia concentrated specifically at the lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Ciliate Wreath Lichen is the only one with prominent white hair-like projections along all lobe edges.
Among its relatives, Hairy Shadow Lichen is distinguished by those characteristic hair-like edge projections that other shadow lichens lack.

Unlike its relatives such as Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange inner tissues) or Hairy Shadow Lichen (which has fuzzy edges), Mealy Shadow Lichen lacks both colorful internal tissues and hairy margins.

Unlike its relatives like Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange interiors) or Mealy Shadow Lichen (which has white powdery surfaces), Red-cored Starburst Shadow Lichen is the only species in its genus with the distinctive crimson interior.
Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Whiskered Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its particularly prominent marginal cilia and small size.
Among its shadow lichen relatives, Scaly Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its prominently curled, squarrose lobes that create a three-dimensional texture.
